title: Analyzing news engagement on Facebook: tracking ideological segregation and news quality in the Facebook URL dataset
screen_reason: Aggregate behavioural analysis of the Facebook Privacy-Protected Full URLs Dataset (US, Jan 2017 - Dec 2020). Reports the proportion of clicks (consumption) directed at low-quality/unreliable news domains, i.e. an exposure share of the news diet with a stated denominator (clicks on 1,231 popular news domains). Unreliable-source measures are in scope per the broad misinformation definition.

estimates.measure_type: % of clicks on popular news URLs that went to low-quality (untrustworthy) news domains
estimates.value_raw: fluctuates around 20% and 30%; at the post-2020 rebound "achieving values similar to the start of the plot, with 30% of the engagement directed towards low-quality sources"
estimates.denominator: All clicks by US Facebook users on URLs from the 1,231 popular news domains analysed (6,273,432 news URLs, Jan 2017-Dec 2020); total click count not reported
estimates.definition: A click counts toward the numerator when the clicked URL's domain has a composite quality score below the low-quality threshold (quality bin below the bin centred at 0.58; Tlow = 0.6, aligned with NewsGuard's trustworthiness cutoff)
estimates.misinfo_def: "our use of the term 'misinformation' throughout this work refers to a broad behavioral pattern of spreading false or misleading content, and not the narrower, intent-based definition that distinguishes disinformation"
estimates.n: 6,273,432 news URLs across 1,231 news domains (denominator is clicks on these URLs; click count not reported)
estimates.source_quote: We also see an immediate increase after the drops in both cases, even though it is steeper in the second region, achieving values similar to the start of the plot, with 30% of the engagement directed towards low-quality sources.
estimates.page_loc: Section 4.4 (RQ5b), p. 16, with Fig. 5F and Eq. (5)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level composite quality score from Lin et al. (2023), a principal-component composite of six independent expert rating sources including NewsGuard, capturing factual reporting, transparency, editorial standards and an outlet's history of sharing false or misleading content. Threshold Tlow = 0.6 (NewsGuard high-trustworthiness cutoff); the empirical bin boundary used is 0.58. No content-level verification.
estimates.moderator_quote: We also quantify the prevalence of content from low-quality sources, which can be indicative of a higher risk of misinformation exposure, by calculating the proportion of URLs with a content quality score lower than a threshold Tlow [34]. ... (F) shows the proportion of clicks directed towards low-quality domains, Eq. (5) with Tlow = 0.6.
estimates.notes: The paper reports this only as a band read off a monthly time series (Fig. 5F), never as a single headline point, so value_kind is range_not_point and value_pct is empty. The one verbatim point value in the text is 30% (post-March-2020 rebound, similar to the January 2017 level); an adjudicator wanting a poolable point could use 30 for the 2020 rebound, but that is the peak of the band, not a representative average. Denominator is clicks (the authors argue clicks are the more reliable consumption indicator than views); the same analysis with views, shares, likes and comments is said to give qualitatively similar results. Domain set is the top 1% most-viewed US domains that have both ideology and quality scores, hence denom_selection=curated. Engagement counts carry injected differential-privacy noise and only URLs shared >=100 times/month enter the dataset. year set to 2019 as the midpoint of the Jan 2017-Dec 2020 window. Source quote replaced (it was an ellipsis join of two sentences) with the single contiguous sentence that carries the 30% point. The sentence that states the band cannot be quoted: the text rendering of that line lost its inter-word spaces ("whichﬂuctuatesaround 20%and30 %"). It reads, in the paper: "In Fig. 5F we show the change in the proportion of engagement directed at low-quality domains (quality bin lower than the bin centered at 0.58 in Fig. 1), which fluctuates around 20% and 30%." That sentence, not the one quoted, is the basis for coding this row range_not_point 20-30%.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) MAIN JUDGEMENT CALL - a concentration-shaped pair is reported but for ALL content, not misinformation: "We begin with the list of the 2629 most-viewed domains [22], which account for over 77% of all URL views and over 80% of all URL clicks in the U.S. on Facebook from 2017 to 2020", and these 2,629 are described as the "top 1% most-viewed domains" (Table 1 gives 1,231 news + 268,821 other domains, consistent with ~1%). That is a top-1%-of-sources / 77-80%-of-views pair, satisfying R1 formally, but the exposure being concentrated is all URL views, not misinformation exposure, so I did not create a CONCENTRATION row. It is also attached to citation [22] (Buntain et al.), so it may be a figure the paper takes from elsewhere, which R8 forbids. Flagging for adjudication. (2) "approximately 58% have a quality score greater than 0.6, a threshold aligned with NewsGuard's definition of high trustworthiness" is a HIGH-quality share of the 1,231 news domains; the low-quality domain share would be a complement I computed, which R8 forbids, so no row. Note the paper is internally inconsistent here: it then says "the remaining 53% of domains from the original top 1% list", where 53% refers to a different denominator (the 2,629-domain top-1% list, not the 1,231 news domains). (3) Fig. 5A/5D weighted average domain ideology and quality scores by user group are scale scores on 0-1 domain-score scales, not shares of misinformation, so no rows. (4) Total Variation distances, correlations (r = -0.35, r = -0.48) and engagement counts are not prevalence shares. (5) No per-user or per-source concentration of low-quality consumption is reported; the authors explicitly note they cannot do individual-level analysis and that trends "may be driven by a relatively small group of highly active users" - stated as a limitation, with no numbers.

rob.design: Aggregate, longitudinal analysis of the Facebook Privacy-Protected Full URLs Dataset for the US, January 2017 - December 2020, queried monthly with a 3-month post-posting cutoff. Corpus: 1,231 news domains (6,273,432 URLs) formed by intersecting the top 1% most-viewed US domains (2,629 domains, per Buntain et al.) with domains having both Lin et al. quality scores (1,586 of 2,629, ~63%) and Robertson et al. audience-ideology scores (1,664 of 2,629, ~63%); 268,821 'other' domains (5,215,067 URLs) used for comparison. Users stratified by Facebook's internally computed Political Page Affinity (-2 to +2 plus 'not defined'). No individual-level data and no count of unique users. Known data limitations addressed by the authors: differential-privacy noise (they report SNR > 1e5 for noisy denominators and compute worst-case uncertainty intervals), a 100-shares-per-month URL inclusion threshold that may bias toward viral posts, and a documented 2021 data-integrity lapse in which US undefined-PPA engagement was missing. No human coding, hence no inter-coder reliability; classification is entirely domain-list based. Access governed by a Meta Research Data Agreement, limiting replication.
